input.text: You've arrived at Fragrant Hills — the Beijing autumn that everyone talks about. This imperial park at the foot of the Western Mountains has been a retreat since the Jin dynasty, eight hundred years ago — emperors built temples here, and the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors made it a summer escape of palaces and pines. The park's name comes from the hill's twin peaks — said to smell of sweet incense, though what draws the crowds is color: every late October into November, the mountainsides of smoke trees turn crimson, and half of Beijing hikes up to walk inside that red. The climb to Incense Burner Peak — five hundred fifty meters, stairs most of the way — rewards you with the whole Beijing plain at your feet. On the way, visit the Temple of Azure Clouds at the park's edge, where the body of Dr. Sun Yat-sen, father of modern China, lay in state in nineteen twenty-five. Arrive early on autumn weekends — the red leaves deserve your sunrise, not your traffic jam.
